sources.authors: Kevin M. Moroney, Ken O'Connell, Paul Meikle-Janney, Stephen B. G. O'Brien, Gavin M. Walker and William T. Lee
sources.source_byte_caveat: Original publisher HTML directly inspected; publisher PDF/HTML original bytes and raw experiment data not independently SHA-256 hashed.
sources.claims_verified_externally: Experimental 59mm cylindrical chamber: ~90C water, 60g ground coffee, ~1L brew, constant 250mL/min; authors explicitly note that quantities/time are closer to drip filter than ordinary espresso. Two different commercial grinds/coffees rather than controlled same-bean grinder comparison. Cylinder pressure drops ~2.3 bar (fine) and 0.65 bar (coarse) matched that fixture; conical spatial extraction gradients are CFD predictions assuming fixed packing, fully wetted bed and no initial dissolved water solubles, not direct live espresso puck images. Article's 18-22% extraction preference history traces to filter-coffee control chart; no new blinded espresso taste/5-rating outcomes.

sources.title: Influence of the Brewing Temperature on the Taste of Espresso
sources.authors: Johanna A. Klotz, Gertrud Winkler, Dirk W. Lachenmeier
sources.source_byte_caveat: Direct text from original five-page published PDF reproduced by scholarly mirror, crosschecked against first-party MDPI publisher search index and PubMed/PMC. Screenshot endpoint cache miss; no visual PDF certification or original PDF byte SHA-256.
sources.claims_verified_externally: ECM Synchronika machine, one medium-dark Arabica/canephora Orphea blend, 7 +/- 0.5g coffee, target 25 +/- 2.5g drink in 25 +/- 5s, approximately 55C samples for blind triangle tasting. At 24 panelists, 80-v-93C: 11/24 correct, below 13/24 cutoff (not significant); 80-v-128C: 15/24 correct, significant. Experimental variables were machine temperature SETPOINTS, not independently measured actual puck-water temperatures. A negative significance test does not establish sensory equivalence. No blinded hedonic preference, long-term health outcome or multi-coffee machine-generalizable 93C ceiling.

sources.title: Development of a 'living' lexicon for descriptive sensory analysis of brewed coffee
sources.authors: Edgar Chambers IV, Karolina Sanchez, Uyen X. T. Phan, Rhonda Miller, Gail V. Civille and Brizio Di Donfrancesco
sources.source_byte_caveat: Publisher full HTML and original WCR owner resource directly read; HTML/PDF original raw bytes, figures and per-panel source data not independently SHA-256 archived; not evidence of five-slider accuracy or user outcome.
sources.claims_verified_externally: 105 coffees from 14 countries in four sets; development panel five highly trained assessors, with 0-15 intensity reference scales. Methods brewed sets 1/4 with 7g/100mL filtered immersion, sets 2/3 with 3.9 and 5.5g/100mL drip; SOME set 3/4 coffee also on a GS-3 automated espresso machine. Validation used six trained assessors, 20 set-4 samples, three repetitions and 50 selected terms among 110 attribute lexicon; original authors expressly call for espresso-specific sublexicons. WCR official Lexicon 2.0 October 2017 added globally accessible references for 24 attributes including Sour, Bitter and Salty. Neither a five-point all-green consumer taste test nor a causal grind/yield/temperature rule is evaluated.

sources.title: Chemical composition, antioxidant activity, and sensory profile of espresso-based Arabica coffee from different bean origins
sources.authors: Nadia Fitri, Nazwa Nurhaliza, El Syifa Anggraeni, Dian Herawati, Dase Hunaefi, Yulianti and Santi Noviasari
sources.source_byte_caveat: First-party 7-page original publisher PDF text inspected through browser; publisher PDF physical page 3 visually inspected; full binary download failed, no raw PDF SHA-256, supplemental tables or participant-level data validation.
sources.claims_verified_externally: Fixed HeyCafe H1 2.0 grind, 18g dose and Rancilio Silvia Pro; output called 36mL (two 18mL cups), NOT a directly measured 36g mass yield. Three Indonesian origins roasted medium-dark L*26-27, four drink preparations (black espresso and three milk/sugar recipes); 3x4x3 design reports 36 experimental chemistry units. Sensory CATA had 30 volunteer drinkers checking 21 attributes including taste sweet, aftertaste astringent and mouthfeel dry, not a 1-5 five-score espresso dial-in tool. Sugar quantified for Gayo recipe subset only; black espresso sugar reported non-detect in that laboratory assay. Source cannot identify causal isolated origin or grinder adjustment effects, sensory sweetness from measured sugar, clinical benefit or universally optimum temperature/yield.

sources.title: Influence of coffee/water ratio on the final quality of espresso coffee
sources.authors: Susana Andueza, María A. Vila, M. Paz de Peña, Concepción Cid
sources.published: 2007-01-15 version of record; Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture 87(4):586–592
sources.source_byte_caveat: Publisher official abstract and publication history inspected directly; complete original paper/PDF binary, explicit methods/sample sizes, detailed sensory panel, processing controls, statistical tables and actual beverage mass not checked.
sources.claims_verified_externally: Wiley abstract reports comparing coffee/water ratio by botanical variety (Arabica and Robusta) and roast (conventional vs torrefacto). Conditional sensory attributes bitterness, astringency and burnt/acrid/earthy/musty flavors prompted author selection of 6.5 g ground coffee per 40 mL nominal beverage or 7.5 g/40 mL for conventional roast groups, and 6.5 g/40 mL for torrefacto. Authors suggest torrefacto roasted-with-sugar processing may affect acids and melanoidins. These are coffee-dose / beverage-VOLUME comparisons and NOT modern beverage mass ratios, taste-optimal dose formulas or verification that automatically reducing dose improves an individual's modern double-shot espresso.

sources.title: Chemical and Sensorial Characteristics of Espresso Coffee As Affected by Grinding and Torrefacto Roast
sources.authors: Susana Andueza, M. Paz de Peña, Concepción Cid
sources.published: 2003-10-18 online; 2003-11-19 issue, Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry 51(24):7034-7039
sources.source_byte_caveat: Original publisher abstract and PubMed reproduction directly inspected. Full 6-page ACS PDF/methods, actual PSD distributions, grind burr/calibration, panels, randomized/blinded design, uncertainty, raw caffeine/solute/foam observations and raw bytes not verified; ACS charges for full text, no purchase made.
sources.claims_verified_externally: ACS abstract names coarse/fine/very-fine grind classes on two 20% Arabica/80% Robusta blend roast conditions: natural and a condition with 50% of Robusta torrefacto roasted (sugar added during roast). It reports inverse relation between particle size and some solid/volatile extraction; higher foam/EY in torrefacto possibly due to caramelized sugar/melanoidins; its chosen grinding grade was FINE for natural but COARSE for torrefacto. Abstract proposes an acceptable extraction-yield upper bound of 25% for that torrefacto condition only, not a validated universal goal.

sources.title: Influence of particle size distribution on espresso extraction via packed bed compression
sources.authors: Mauricio Vaca Guerra; Yogesh M. Harshe; Lennart Fries; Hannah Sophia Rothberg; Stefan Palzer; Stefan Heinrich
sources.published: Journal of Food Engineering 340, article 111301 (March 2023); DOI string includes online 2022
sources.source_byte_caveat: Publisher DOI and institutional metadata/abstract were read, but the final binary article, methods/figures/tables, any raw trials and response-surface parameters were not obtained. The repository page does not expose a downloadable PDF. DOI landing page returned an access error. Do not equate abstract with full-text analysis or extrapolate to practical grinder setting, tamping instruction or taste improvement.
sources.claims_verified_externally: TU Hamburg author-institution repository abstract reports that at matched axial compression, decreasing coarse-distribution uniformity beta decreased dry bed porosity even when mean particle size alpha was larger. Espresso extraction experiments indicated similarly low permeability can arise from compression, size mean and size uniformity jointly; model predicted porosity/permeability for studied preparations. It DOES NOT establish a quantitative universal espresso grind step, optimal tamp force, five-taste rating threshold, or one-variable next-shot rule.

sources.title: Development of coffee bean porosity and thermophysical properties during roasting
sources.authors: M. Al-Shemmeri; P. Fryer; R. Farr; E. Lopez-Quiroga
sources.source_byte_caveat: Publisher search index exposed original detailed methods and table text; live DOI redirect blocked direct page. No HTML/PDF bytes or figures downloaded/hashed; this is not complete paper certification.
sources.claims_verified_externally: 350 g single Kenyan Arabica regional blend, 0.0228 kg/s air flow, 220/235/250/265/280C inlet temperatures to measured color 70 +/-1; Micro-CT triplicate, 100 cross-sections of 0.76 mm chosen bean region. Time to final color 700s at 220C vs 168s at 280C. Porosity rose approximately 40-60% through roasting, final porosity differs despite matched color; larger differences at 280C versus 220-265C. Authors explicitly excluded flavor chemistry/sensory studies; some partial-roast porosity observations had SE ~4.6%.

sources.title: Direct electrochemical appraisal of black coffee quality using cyclic voltammetry
sources.authors: Robin E. Bumbaugh; Doran L. Pennington; Lena C. Wehn; Elias J. Rheingold; Joshua R. Williams; Benjamin J. Aleman; Christopher H. Hendon
sources.source_byte_caveat: Primary publisher HTML directly reviewed; no raw HTML/PDF byte download or SHA-256, no raw Figshare dataset or supplemental figure re-analysis. A roaster's preregistered sensory QC label is not a new controlled consumer taste preference trial.
sources.claims_verified_externally: One Colombian coffee in six roasts Agtron 75.8 to 55.7, rested seven days, EK43 ground, SCA cupped at 1:13.5 with 93 C water for 4 min and V60-filtered, analyzed cool (21.6 C), NOT espresso. CV Pt electrode measured roast- and TDS-sensitive charge; calibration is coffee-conditional. Four batches of a different same-spec coffee (three accepted, one light rejected Agtron 98.9 against target 93+/-1) were provided single-blind to investigators, each batch brewed five times. First-cycle CV separated the rejected batch while TDS did not; n=5 denotes within-batch preparations, NOT independent coffees or human assessors. No five-score user taste intervention, espresso grinder tuning or optimal beverage recipe established.

sources.title: Time-resolved extraction of caffeine and trigonelline from finely-ground espresso coffee with varying particle sizes and tamping pressures
sources.authors: Michael Kuhn; Sandra Lang; Franziska Bezold; Mirjana Minceva; Heiko Briesen

Tested tamp-pressure values and uncertainty intervals not verified from full text.
sources.source_byte_caveat: Only institution-hosted original abstract/bibliography was read; no direct publisher manuscript/PDF, tables or original bytes retrieved or hashed. Does not prove tamp force never affects extraction, hydraulic flow, taste or style-specific outcomes.

Pages 22-25 chart a 12 bar peak Golden Profile and historical shop examples with lower 6 bar peak for higher-solubility/darker and 9 bar for intermediate coffees; author says one profile is not best for every coffee. These are machine-specific practitioner examples without presented trial n, blinded sensory, uncertainty or general brew-pressure optimum.

sources.title: Moisture-controlled triboelectrification during coffee grinding
sources.authors: Joshua Mendez Harper; Connor S. McDonald; Elias J. Rheingold; Lena C. Wehn; Robin E. Bumbaugh; and coauthors
sources.claims_verified_externally: Authors report roast shade and grind coarseness influence electrical charge, residual bean moisture can change charge magnitude and polarity, and external water reduced charge/clumping and altered espresso flow in studied conditions. They describe a likely taste implication but not independently verified universal taste improvement or grinder-specific adjustment magnitude.
sources.source_byte_caveat: Primary manuscript and figures not obtained or hashed. The independent 2024 iScience mitigation paper DOI 10.1016/j.isci.2024.110639 is a DISTINCT follow-on experiment already indexed as LIT-2024-RDT-ISCIENCE; do not attribute its >=15% darker-roast espresso beverage-concentration measurement to this Matter abstract.

sources.title: Sensory profile of Italian Espresso brewed Arabica Specialty Coffee under three roasting profiles with chemical and safety insight on roasted beans

Authors report medium roast often better preserved expected source cupping descriptors under that tested espresso preparation, not a universal objectively optimal roast, recipe, extraction time, temperature or app taste threshold.
